content: Differentiating typhoid fever caused by Salmonella Typhi and paratyphoid fever caused by Salmonella Paratyphi A from other febrile illnesses in endemic regions is diagnostically challenging. Although rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for enteric fever are commercially available as alternatives to blood or bone marrow culture (the current reference standard) or the Widal test, their diagnostic accuracy remains uncertain. If proven accurate, these RDTs could potentially replace blood culture as the World Health Organization (WHO)-recommended primary diagnostic test for enteric fever. The objective of this study was to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of commercially available RDTs and prototype tests for detecting Salmonella Typhi or Salmonella Paratyphi A infections in symptomatic individuals residing in endemic areas. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, up to March 4, 2016. Additional sources, such as WHO reports, conference papers, and test manufacturers, were also consulted to identify relevant studies. The inclusion criteria focused on diagnostic accuracy studies of RDTs for enteric fever in febrile patients or those with symptoms suggestive of enteric fever in endemic regions. The reference standards were classified as Grade 1 (blood culture and bone marrow culture) or Grade 2 (blood culture combined with blood polymerase chain reaction or blood culture alone). Data extraction and quality assessment were performed independently by two reviewers using a modified QUADAS-2 tool. Meta-analyses were conducted when sufficient studies were available, and heterogeneity was reasonable. A total of 37 studies, involving 5080 participants, met the inclusion criteria. The prevalence of enteric fever in the study populations ranged from 1% to 75%, with a median prevalence of 24%. Sixteen different RDTs were evaluated, with 16 studies comparing two or more RDTs. Only three studies used the Grade 1 reference standard, and only 11 studies included unselected febrile patients. Most studies were conducted in Asia, with five studies from sub-Saharan Africa. The majority of RDTs were designed to detect Salmonella Typhi only. The three most commonly evaluated RDTs were TUBEX (14 studies), Typhidot and its variants (22 studies), and the Test-It Typhoid immunochromatographic lateral flow assay and its prototypes (9 studies). Meta-analyses revealed the following diagnostic performance: TUBEX: Average sensitivity of 78% (95% CI: 71%-85%) and specificity of 87% (95% CI: 82%-91%). Test-It Typhoid and prototypes (KIT): Average sensitivity of 69% (95% CI: 59%-78%) and specificity of 90% (95% CI: 78%-93%). Typhidot (all forms): Average sensitivity of 84% (95% CI: 73%-91%) and specificity of 79% (95% CI: 70%-87%). When analyzing the 13 Typhidot studies that either reported indeterminate results or used test formats without indeterminate results, the sensitivity was 78% (95% CI: 65%-87%) and specificity was 77% (95% CI: 66%-86%). No significant differences in sensitivity or specificity were observed between TUBEX, Typhidot, and Test-It Typhoid tests when compared to these 13 Typhidot studies. However, when comparing TUBEX and Test-It Typhoid to all Typhidot studies, Typhidot demonstrated higher sensitivity than Test-It Typhoid by 15% (95% CI: 2%-28%), though other comparisons showed no significant differences. In a hypothetical cohort of 1000 febrile patients, where 30% (300 patients) have enteric fever: Typhidot (with or without indeterminate results) would miss 66 cases of enteric fever and falsely diagnose 161 individuals without the disease. TUBEX would miss 66 cases and falsely diagnose 91 individuals without the disease. Test-It Typhoid and prototypes (KIT) would miss 93 cases and falsely diagnose 70 individuals without the disease. The confidence intervals for these estimates were wide, and no significant differences in false-positive rates were observed between the tests. The quality of the included studies was assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool, and the overall certainty of the evidence was deemed low. In conclusion, the 37 studies evaluating the diagnostic accuracy of RDTs for enteric fever revealed moderate diagnostic performance for the three main RDTs and their variants. There was no significant difference in the average sensitivity and specificity among the three tests. Further robust evaluations of alternative RDTs for enteric fever are necessary to improve diagnostic accuracy.
